lessons.title: Rough offal and separating it from the carcass
lessons.html:
What rough offal is

Rough offal is the stomach and intestines (the gut or tripe and casings), plus parts such as the feet and head in some abattoirs. It is called rough because it holds dung and food in the gut, so it is the dirtiest part of the animal after the hide. Many people in South Africa buy tripe, trotters and heads (for example mogodu, trotters and sheep heads), so rough offal is a real product with value.

Taking out the gut (evisceration)

When the gut is taken out of the carcass it must not be cut or torn. One cut in the gut can spill dung all over the carcass. That carcass must then be trimmed heavily or may be condemned.

  • The food pipe (weasand) and the back passage (bung) are tied or clipped before the gut comes out. This stops spillage.
  • The gut set falls into the gut tray or gut truck, not onto the floor.
  • The gut set stays linked to its carcass number until the meat inspector has looked at it.

Keep dirty and clean apart

Rough offal is handled in a separate room, the gut room. Workers in this area must not go to the clean meat area without washing hands, changing apron and using the boot wash. Gut trays and trolleys from the gut room do not go into the clean area.

Inspection

The meat inspector checks the stomachs, intestines and lymph glands for disease and worms. Only after the inspector passes them may you start to empty and clean them. Condemned parts go into the condemned bin.

lessons.title: Emptying, cleaning and chilling rough offal
lessons.html:
Emptying, cleaning and chilling

Separating the gut set

  1. Separate the stomachs from the intestines.
  2. For cattle and sheep, separate the four stomach parts as your abattoir instructs.
  3. Pull the fat off the intestines if it is saved, and put it in its own clean container.

Emptying

  • Cut open the stomachs over the emptying table or drain so the contents fall straight into the waste chute.
  • Squeeze or strip out the intestine contents into the waste chute.
  • Keep the contents away from cleaned products.
  • Stomach contents go to the waste or compost area. They must not run into rivers or the veld. Follow your abattoir waste rules.

Washing and cleaning

  1. Rinse the emptied tripe with plenty of clean water.
  2. Scald or wash in the tripe washer at the temperature and time set by your supervisor.
  3. Check that no dung, food or slime is left.
  4. Trim off damaged or dirty bits.

Cooling and packing

  • Cool the cleaned offal quickly in cold water or the chiller.
  • Pack in clean containers, labelled with the date.
  • Store in the chiller. Rough offal spoils quickly.

Safety in the gut room

  • The floor is wet and slippery. Wear boots with a good grip and keep drains clear.
  • Hot water and scalding machines burn. Do not put your hands into the machine while it runs. Switch off and lock out before you clean or clear a jam.
  • Keep your knife sharp, cut away from yourself, and sterilise it often.
  • Gut contents can carry germs. Cover cuts, wear gloves and wash hands well.

Key points

  • Rough offal is the stomachs, intestines and parts like feet and heads.
  • A torn gut spills dung on the carcass, so remove the gut carefully.
  • Handle rough offal in the gut room, separate from clean meat.
  • Clean only offal that the inspector has passed.
  • Empty, wash well, chill quickly and label.
